VOLUME 5

Pre-training

From raw text to a trained base model. The next-token objective, data pipelines, tokenization, the training loop, scaling laws with real FLOPs math, and what a real multi-week run looks and feels like.

Last verified: September 2026. Live-verified against public sources:
  • FineWeb: about 15T tokens from 96 Common Crawl dumps (HuggingFaceFW dataset card).
  • Chinchilla 70B on 1.4T tokens and Gopher 280B on 300B tokens (Hoffmann et al., arXiv:2203.15556, 2022).
  • GPT-3 3.14e23 training FLOPs (Brown et al., 2020, Table D.1).
  • LLaMA-2 2T tokens with a 4M-token global batch (Meta model card).
  • LLaMA-3 15T+ tokens (Meta, 2024).
  • A100 312 TFLOPS FP16 tensor throughput (NVIDIA).
  • PaLM loss-spike restart protocol, about 20 spikes on the 540B run (Chowdhery et al., 2022).

FLOP and budget arithmetic: re-computed on this machine. Capstone tiny-GPT lab: executed on this machine (PyTorch 2.14.0 CPU). UNVERIFIED: none.

1. The pre-training objective: next-token prediction

Pre-training is one simple task, repeated trillions of times. The task: predict the next token.

Design prompt

  • "What exactly does the model learn to predict? Write the loss for one sequence."
  • "How does one forward pass produce a prediction for every position? Draw the shift."
  • "What is the loss of a model that guesses uniformly at random with a 32k vocabulary?"

The three nouns this chapter stands on. A token is a chunk of text the model reads as one unit, usually a word piece like "cat" or "ing". The tokenizer (Volume 4, Chapter 1) cuts raw text into tokens. It maps each distinct token to an integer ID. The full set of IDs is the vocabulary (32,000 entries in this chapter's running example). Training means adjusting the model's parameters (the billions of numbers inside it) so its predictions get better.

Everything below shows the machinery that does that adjustment well.

How to read this diagram

  1. Left: raw text ("the cat sat on the"), cut into tokens, each mapped to an integer ID.
  2. Middle: the transformer reads the IDs and outputs one probability distribution over the whole vocabulary.
  3. Right: the bars show the leading candidates. The true next token ("mat") gets 0.62, highlighted.
  4. Bottom: the loss for this position is -log(0.62) = 0.48 nats. Repeat for every position of every sequence, trillions of times: that is pre-training.

Step 1: predict the next token

The pre-training objective is next-token prediction, also called causal language modeling. Given tokens 1 through t, predict token t+1. The model's final layer outputs a probability distribution over the entire vocabulary. That is 32,000 numbers summing to 1. Training rewards putting probability on the token that actually came next. That is the entire objective.

The model learns everything as a side effect of this one task: grammar, Python, trivia. Predicting well requires understanding.

Step 2: why this task works

Three properties make it uniquely powerful. First, supervision is free: any text carries its own labels (the label for position t is token t+1). No human annotation, so it scales to trillions of tokens. Second, it is dense: every single token position is a training example, so a 4,096-token sequence yields 4,096 gradient signals per forward pass. Third, it is general: to predict the next token of arbitrary text, the model must learn syntax, facts, reasoning patterns, and style. A narrower task (classify sentiment) would teach a narrower model.

Step 3: the shift trick and cross-entropy

Take a sequence of n tokens: [t1, t2, t3, ..., tn]. (Chapter 3 shows how raw documents become fixed-length sequences.) One forward pass produces n output distributions, one per position.

The trick: position i predicts token i+1. The inputs are tokens 1..n-1. The targets are tokens 2..n. Same sequence, shifted by one. The causal mask (Volume 4, Chapter 3) guarantees position i never sees token i+1, so the prediction is honest.

tokens:   t1    t2    t3    t4  ...  tn
           |     |     |     |
input:   [ t1 | t2 | t3 | ... | t(n-1) ]   -> model -> n-1 distributions
target:  [ t2 | t3 | t4 | ... | tn     ]   (each position predicts the next token)

loss = average over positions of  -log( p_model(correct token) )
     = cross-entropy between the true next token and the model's distribution

Cross-entropy here is the same concept as Volume 1. For a single correct token c, the loss is -log p(c). Here p(c) is the probability the model assigned it. Confident and right: p = 0.9 gives loss 0.105. Confident and wrong: p = 0.01 gives loss 4.6. We measure loss in nats: the unit of information when you use the natural logarithm (bits are the same idea with log base 2).

The logarithm punishes confident mistakes far more than mild uncertainty. That is why training drives the model toward calibrated probabilities rather than wild guesses.

How to read this diagram

  1. Horizontal axis: the probability the model assigned to the correct next token. Vertical axis: the loss contribution, in nats.
  2. The curve's shape: extremely steep near zero, flat near one. The first improvements (from random guessing to vaguely sensible) erase most of the loss. The last improvements (from good to near-certain) barely move it.
  3. Why it matters for reading loss curves (Chapter 6): loss falls fast early. The model climbs the steep part: it learns basic statistics like "the most common tokens". Late training grinds on the flat part: genuinely hard predictions.

Step 4: what loss values mean

A model guessing uniformly over a 32,000-token vocabulary assigns p = 1/32000 to the correct token. Its loss is -log(1/32000) = ln(32000) = 10.37 nats. This is the starting line: an untrained model reports ~10.4. A well-trained base model lands around 1.8 to 2.2 nats on held-out text. Perplexity, the traditional language-modeling metric, is just e^loss. Loss 2.0 means perplexity 7.4.

Read that as "the model is as confused as if choosing uniformly among 7.4 tokens". Lower is better. Perplexity converts the abstract nats into something with units of choice.

Common misunderstanding: "the model trains to predict the next word correctly, like a quiz." It trains to match a distribution. For "the cat sat on the ___", both "mat" and "floor" are valid. The loss rewards putting probability on all plausible continuations in proportion to their frequency. It does not reward picking one winner. A model that always guessed the single most likely token would have higher loss than one that spreads probability correctly. This distributional view is also why sampling temperature (Volume 8) works: the model learned a distribution, and generation samples from it.
Field relevance: the objective question is fundamental enough that reviewers ask it as a warm-up, and deep enough to carry follow-ups. The strong candidate writes -log p(correct) immediately. The candidate draws the shift. The candidate computes the uniform baseline (10.37 for 32k vocab) unprompted. The candidate defines perplexity as e to the loss. The distributional correction ("not a quiz, a distribution match") shows real understanding.

Key takeaways

  • Pre-training = next-token prediction on every position of every training sequence. Supervision is free, dense, and general.
  • One forward pass yields n-1 predictions via the shifted input/target trick. The causal mask keeps it honest.
  • Loss per position is -log p(correct token). Uniform guessing over 32k tokens gives 10.37 nats. Trained models reach ~2.
  • Perplexity = e^loss. The model learns a distribution over continuations, not a single answer.
Forward link: the next chapter asks where the trillions of training tokens come from. It shows how raw web text becomes clean, deduplicated training data. The loss defined here is the y-axis of every scaling plot in Chapter 7.

How to read this diagram

  1. Top: the full 6-token sequence, each token with its position number.
  2. Middle (blue): the input to the model: positions 1 to 5.
  3. Bottom (amber): the target labels: positions 2 to 6.
  4. Arrows: each input predicts the target directly below it. Position 3 (sat) predicts position 4 (on).
  5. Not drawn: the causal mask, which stops each position from seeing its own target.

How to read this diagram

  1. Axes: horizontal is the probability the model gave the correct token. Vertical is the loss in nats.
  2. Shape: the curve falls steeply on the left and flattens on the right.
  3. Red dot (0.01, 4.61): a near-blind guess. Very expensive.
  4. Amber dot (0.1, 2.30): ten times more confident, 2.3 nats cheaper. This is where early training lives.
  5. Green dots: late training. Going from 0.8 to 0.9 saves only 0.12 nats. The grind is real.

2. Where training data comes from

Petabytes of web crawl in, filtered tokens out. The pipeline nobody sees and everybody depends on.

Chapter 1 defined the objective, next-token prediction. It left a big question open: prediction of what? This chapter answers it. It shows where the trillions of training tokens come from. It shows how raw web text becomes clean, deduplicated training data.

Design prompt

  • "Where do pre-training tokens come from? Why is the web the only viable source at trillion-token scale?"
  • "What does a data pipeline do between the raw crawl and the tokenizer? Name the stages and what each removes."
  • "Why is deduplication important? What goes wrong if you skip it?"

Step 1: the scale of the problem

A pre-training dataset is a collection of text, measured in tokens. It is large enough that a model can learn language, facts, and reasoning patterns from it by next-token prediction (Chapter 1). Modern datasets run to trillions of tokens. For reference, the public FineWeb dataset contains 15 trillion tokens. No human-curated collection reaches that scale. The only source big enough is the web, harvested by crawlers.

Step 2: the raw material

Common Crawl is a nonprofit that has crawled the public web monthly since 2007. It publishes the results as free multi-petabyte archives. Each monthly crawl is hundreds of terabytes of raw HTML. It is noisy: navigation menus, ads, cookie banners, SEO spam, machine-generated filler, duplicated articles syndicated across hundreds of sites. Raw Common Crawl is not a training set. It is the ore.

Everything in this chapter is the refinery.

Why the web and not books or curated corpora? Arithmetic. A large library of books is tens of billions of tokens. Chinchilla-optimal training of a 70B model needs 1.4 trillion tokens (Chapter 7). Only the web has that much text. Teams must use even the web nearly whole.

That is why data quality work matters so much. At this scale you cannot hand-check anything, so the pipeline's filters are your quality control.

How to read this diagram

  1. Left labels: four corpora, from books to FineWeb, with the token count each can supply.
  2. Bar length: logarithmic, so each step is roughly a factor of ten. The books bar is a sliver next to Chinchilla's need.
  3. The takeaway: no curated collection reaches trillion-token scale. The web is the only viable source. That is why the pipeline's filters are the quality control.

Step 3: the pipeline, stage by stage

How to read this diagram

  1. Crawl: raw HTML from Common Crawl plus targeted sources (code from GitHub, papers, books). Mostly noise at this point.
  2. Filter: extract main text (drop menus, ads, boilerplate). Keep the target languages. Apply heuristic rules: drop documents with too many repeated lines, too high a symbol-to-word ratio, too few words, or blocklisted content. Each rule is cheap and each removes a visible failure class.
  3. Dedup: remove exact duplicates, then near-duplicates (fuzzy matching, below). The most compute-efficient stage in the pipeline: every duplicate removed is training compute not wasted.
  4. Quality: score what remains and mix sources deliberately. High-signal text (reference articles, books, code) gets upweighted. The final blend is a designed data mixture, not whatever survived.
  5. Tokenize: run the BPE tokenizer (Volume 4, Chapter 1) over the final text to produce the integer sequences training actually consumes.

Here is what breaks if you skip a stage. Skip filtering and the model learns cookie-banner prose as a major dialect. Skip dedup and the model memorizes duplicated content. It wastes a measurable fraction of the compute budget re-learning it. Skip the quality mix and capabilities skew toward whatever the web overproduces.

Step 4: deduplication, the quiet giant

Duplication on the web is extreme. Publishers syndicate the same article across sites. The same license header sits in every file. The same template text appears on millions of pages. Training on duplicates has two costs. First, wasted compute: every repeated token is gradient steps spent re-learning what the model already knows.

Second, memorization: models trained on heavily duplicated text memorize and regurgitate it. That is both a quality problem and, for sensitive text, a privacy problem.

Two levels, in order:

  1. Exact dedup: hash every document (or every long substring) and drop repeats. Cheap, catches syndication.
  2. Fuzzy (near) dedup: catch documents that are almost identical: same article with a different headline, the same code with renamed variables. The standard tool is MinHash. A small signature of its least-hashed shingles summarizes each document (short substrings). The pipeline treats documents with similar signatures as duplicates. This catches the near-copies exact hashing misses. Near-copies are the bulk of web duplication.

How to read this diagram

  1. Left: three documents. Doc A and Doc B differ by one word ("jumps" vs "leaps"). Doc C is unrelated.
  2. Middle: the pipeline hashes each document's shingles, and the signature keeps the smallest values. A and B share most of theirs. C shares none.
  3. Right: similar signatures mean near-duplicates: keep one copy. A different signature means unique text: keep it.

Step 5: quality and the mixture

After filtering and dedup, teams score documents for educational value: does this text teach something? The FineWeb work showed that classifier-based quality filtering beats heuristic-only pipelines on downstream benchmarks. Here a small model scores documents and keeps the top slice. The surviving text is then blended into a designed mixture. Mostly web, plus meaningful fractions of code (code teaches precise reasoning and structure), books and reference text (dense knowledge), and sometimes synthetic or curated sets. The mixture is a hyperparameter: change it and the model's strengths change.

More code, better reasoning benchmarks. Teams tune this empirically. The exact recipes are among the most guarded secrets in the industry.

How to read this diagram

  1. The bar: what fraction of training batches came from each source, by sampling weight.
  2. The point: change the blend and the model's strengths change: more code shifts it toward reasoning, more books toward dense knowledge.
  3. The caveat: this is one published recipe from 2020. Current labs do not publish their exact mixtures.
Common misunderstanding: "more data is always better." At fixed quality, more tokens help (Chapter 7). But a trillion tokens of spam teach the model to be spam. The last few years of dataset work point one way: aggressive filtering and dedup beat raw scale. FineWeb's headline result was that 15T tokens of filtered web text trained better models than larger unfiltered piles. Quality is not the enemy of scale. At trillion-token scale, quality is the scaling strategy.
Field relevance: data questions test systems thinking about the unglamorous 90% of training. The strong candidate walks the five stages. The candidate explains why dedup saves compute (not just disk). The candidate names MinHash for fuzzy dedup. The candidate says the mixture is a tuned hyperparameter. "Quality filtering beats raw scale" is the current-era sentence.

Key takeaways

  • Pre-training data starts as Common Crawl web ore. The pipeline refines it through filter, dedup, quality, tokenize.
  • Dedup (exact + fuzzy MinHash) saves compute and prevents memorization. It is the highest-ROI stage.
  • Quality filtering and the designed data mixture determine the model's strengths. Teams tune recipes; they are not accidental.
  • FineWeb: 15T filtered tokens, a public reference point for what "clean web scale" looks like.
Forward link: the next chapter takes this clean text. It turns it into the packed, padded, batched integer sequences the training loop consumes.

How to read this diagram

  1. Rows: eight documents, each with its educational value score.
  2. Dashed line: the cutoff at 0.60.
  3. Green dots: kept. The text becomes training tokens.
  4. Red dots: dropped. The text never becomes tokens.
  5. What breaks: set the threshold too high and you starve the model of data. Too low and junk teaches the model junk.

3. Tokenization at scale, packing, and batching

From documents to the fixed-shape tensors a GPU can actually multiply.

Chapter 2 ends with clean text, but the training loop cannot eat text. This chapter is the bridge to tensors. It covers tokenizing at scale, packing documents, and batching into the rectangular inputs that Chapter 4's loop consumes.

Design prompt

  • "Documents have wildly different lengths. How do you turn them into fixed-size training batches?"
  • "What is packing, and what does it do to attention across document boundaries?"
  • "How many tokens are in a typical large-run batch? Show how batch size interacts with the learning rate."

Step 1: from documents to tensors

Training hardware processes rectangular batches: every sequence in a batch must have the same length. Real documents do not cooperate: one is 40 tokens, the next is 12,000. This chapter is the bridge from variable-length documents to the fixed [batch, seq_len] integer tensors the model trains on. Three operations: tokenize everything, pack documents into full-length rows, batch rows into steps.

How to read this diagram

  1. Left box: documents as bars of different lengths, the raw material after tokenization.
  2. Middle boxes: the integer stream, then fixed rows. The red ticks on the rows are document boundaries inside packed sequences.
  3. Bottom: B rows stack into one rectangular tensor. Nothing variable-length survives past packing.

Step 2: packing, precisely

Take the tokenized documents. Concatenate them with a separator token between documents. The separator is usually the end-of-sequence token, a special marker that means one document ends here. Chop the long stream into rows of exactly seq_len (the context length, e.g. 4,096). Each row is one training sequence, typically containing several whole documents plus fragments.

If the final row is short, pad it.

How to read this diagram

  1. Top: four documents as colored bars of different lengths. This is the raw material after tokenization.
  2. Arrow: concatenation with separators, then slicing every 4,096 tokens (illustrative row length here).
  3. Bottom: two full rows. Row 1 holds documents 1 and 2 plus the start of document 3. Row 2 holds the rest plus padding (gray) filling the tail.
  4. The teaching point: padding is nearly eliminated. Without packing, the pipeline would pad each document individually to the longest in the batch. That would waste most of the compute on pad tokens.
documents (token counts):   [1200] [3000] [500] [2600] [900] ...
                                 | concatenate with separators
stream:  d1 | d2 | d3 | d4 | d5 | ...
                                 | slice every 4096
rows:    [==== 4096 tokens ====]   <- docs 1,2 and part of 3
         [==== 4096 tokens ====]   <- rest of 3, docs 4,5, ...
         [==== 4096 tokens ====]
         [== 1800 tokens ==][pad]  <- only the LAST row pads

The subtlety: attention inside a packed row crosses document boundaries. The end of document 1 can attend to the start of document 2, which is meaningless. In practice, large runs mostly accept this. The separator token gives the model a hint. Boundary-crossing attention is a small fraction of all pairs. Some pipelines add explicit document masking.

Know the tradeoff exists. Know the field's default is to accept it.

Step 3: batching and tokens per step

A batch is the set of rows processed in one optimizer step. The number that matters is tokens per batch = rows x seq_len. Large runs use enormous batches: LLaMA used 4 million tokens per batch. Why so large? Two reasons. First, hardware efficiency.

GPUs need big matrix multiplications to stay busy. Tiny batches starve them. Second, gradient noise. The gradient estimated from 4M tokens is far less noisy than from 4K. That stabilizes training. Up to a point, it allows larger learning rates.

But no GPU holds 4M tokens at once. The trick is gradient accumulation (full treatment in Chapter 4). Process small micro-batches that fit in memory. Sum their gradients. Take one optimizer step after enough micro-batches. The model cannot tell the difference between one giant batch and many accumulated micro-batches.

There is one exception: normalization layers. LLMs barely use normalization across the batch (RMSNorm is per-token).

Common misunderstanding: "each training example is one document." After packing, a training sequence is a concatenation of document fragments. The model never sees a clean "one document per example" structure at scale. This matters when people reason about what the model learns. It learns from token streams with arbitrary document boundaries inside them. That is part of why base models are fluent but structurally loose until post-training (Chapter 9, Volume 7).
Field relevance: packing questions test whether you have thought about the data path, not just the model. The strong candidate explains why the pipeline needs rectangles. The candidate draws the pack-and-slice. The candidate names the boundary-attention tradeoff. The candidate connects batch size to gradient noise and hardware utilization. "4M tokens per batch via gradient accumulation" is the scale sentence.

Key takeaways

  • GPUs need fixed-shape batches. Packing (concatenate, slice to seq_len) converts variable documents to full rows with almost no padding.
  • Packed rows mix documents. Practitioners accept boundary-crossing attention as a small cost.
  • What matters is tokens per batch (millions at scale). Teams reach it via gradient accumulation over micro-batches.
  • Large batches: better hardware utilization, less gradient noise, room for larger learning rates.
Looking back: these packed batches feed the objective from Chapter 1: next-token prediction scored with cross-entropy.
Forward link: the next chapter opens the black box of those batches. It shows what one training step actually does, and what it costs in time and memory.

How to read this diagram

  1. Top: the multiplication that defines the batch, 1024 x 4096 = 4M tokens.
  2. Bottom: eight micro-batches, each small enough for memory, summed by gradient accumulation.
  3. The takeaway: gradient noise falls with tokens per step, which is why the batch is enormous even though the hardware sees it in pieces.

4. The training loop: anatomy of one step

Forward, backward, update. What each phase costs in time and memory.

Chapters 2 and 3 built the data pipeline. It ends at packed integer batches. This chapter opens the black box that consumes them. It shows what one training step actually does, and what it costs in time and memory.

Design prompt

  • "Walk me through one training step. Where does the time go, and where does the memory go?"
  • "Why is the backward pass roughly twice the forward pass?"
  • "A 7B model in bf16 (brain float 16, a 2-byte floating-point format; Volume 3) with AdamW: how much memory for weights, gradients, and optimizer states?"

Step 1: what one step is

A training step takes one batch of packed sequences (Chapter 3) and nudges every parameter once. Four phases, in a fixed loop, hundreds of thousands of times:

How to read this diagram

  1. Forward (blue): the batch flows through the model. Logits are the model's raw, unnormalized scores for each vocabulary entry, before they become probabilities. The model computes the logits and the cross-entropy loss (Chapter 1). Cost ~2N FLOPs per token. The backward pass needs them, so every layer's activations stay in memory.
  2. Loss (rose): a single number summarizing the batch. Also the moment any NaN checks fire: a NaN here means something already broke upstream.
  3. Backward (amber): backpropagation (Volume 1) computes a gradient for every parameter. Cost ~4N FLOPs per token, roughly twice the forward. Each layer needs gradients for both its inputs and its weights.
  4. Update (teal): the optimizer (AdamW, from Volume 3) turns gradients into parameter changes, scaled by the learning rate (Chapter 5). Then it zeroes the gradients and the loop repeats.

Here is what breaks if a phase is wrong. A bug in the loss (e.g., forgetting the shift) trains the model to copy instead of predict. Loss still falls, silently. A missing zero-grad accumulates gradients across steps. That looks like a mysteriously effective larger batch until it diverges.

Step 2: what a step costs: time

Per-step FLOPs = 6 x N x (tokens per batch). Worked example, 7B model, 4M-token batch:

FLOPs/step = 6 x 7e9 x 4e6 = 1.68e17 FLOPs

On 256 A100s at 40% MFU (model FLOPs utilization: the fraction of the GPU's rated throughput the run actually achieves; illustrative):
  throughput = 256 x 312e12 x 0.40 = 3.2e16 FLOP/s
  seconds/step = 1.68e17 / 3.2e16 = 5.25 s per step

A 2T-token run at 4M tokens/batch = 500,000 steps.
500,000 steps x 5.25 s = 729 cluster-hours; x 256 GPUs = ~187,000 GPU-hours = ~21 GPU-years.
That is why the batch is huge and the cluster is huge: the step count is fixed
by the token budget, so throughput per step is everything.

How to read this diagram

  1. Read left to right: FLOPs per step, cluster throughput, seconds per step, total for the run.
  2. Each box shows the formula on top and the evaluated number below in bold.
  3. The takeaway: ~187,000 GPU-hours is ~21 GPU-years. The token budget fixes the step count, so throughput per step is everything.

Step 3: what a step costs: memory

Memory per step has four residents. Worked for a 7B model, bf16 weights (2 bytes/param), AdamW (Volume 3):

ResidentBytes per param7B totalNotes
Weights214 GBbf16. The smallest resident.
Gradients214 GBSame shape as weights, usually bf16/fp16.
Optimizer states856 GBAdamW keeps two fp32 numbers per param (momentum, variance). The largest resident.
Activationsvaries10s of GBGrows with batch x seq_len x layers. Saved for backward. Recomputation trades compute for memory (Volume 6).

The surprise for newcomers: the optimizer states dwarf the model. A "7B model" needs ~85 GB just for weights, gradients, and states, before a single activation. That is why training a 7B model does not fit on one 80 GB GPU without sharding. That is why Volume 6 (distributed training) exists. ZeRO and FSDP split the 56 GB of optimizer states across GPUs.

How to read this diagram

  1. The bar: four segments sized by gigabytes. The rose segment (optimizer states) dominates.
  2. The green marker: the 80 GB ceiling of an H100. The bar runs past it before counting activations.
  3. The takeaway: a 7B model does not fit on one 80 GB GPU. ZeRO and FSDP exist specifically to split the 56 GB of optimizer states across GPUs (Volume 6).

Step 4: the supporting cast: accumulation, clipping, precision

  • Gradient accumulation (Chapter 3): run K micro-batches, sum gradients, update once. The optimizer step sees the full 4M-token batch while each GPU holds a fraction. Mathematically identical to one giant batch for the gradient sum (normalization layers aside).

    • How to read this diagram

    1. Top row: four micro-batches, each small enough for one GPU, each producing its own gradients.
    2. Middle: the loop sums the gradients into an accumulator. No optimizer step happens yet.
    3. Right: one optimizer step on the summed gradients. Effective batch: four micro-batches. Memory: one.
  • Gradient clipping: cap the global gradient norm at a threshold (often 1.0). One bad batch can produce an enormous gradient that undoes hours of training. Clipping bounds the damage of any single step. Cheap insurance, nearly universal.
  • Mixed precision (Volume 3): compute in bf16, keep a fp32 master copy of weights. Halves memory traffic and doubles math throughput on modern GPUs. Loss scaling is largely unnecessary in bf16 (its wide exponent range avoids fp16's overflow problems). That is one reason the field standardized on bf16.
Common misunderstanding: "a training step processes one batch, and the batch is what fits on the GPU." At scale these are three different things. The micro-batch is what fits on one GPU. The batch is what one optimizer step covers, via accumulation. The accumulation count relates them. Confusing them makes every throughput and memory calculation wrong by the accumulation factor.
Field relevance: "walk me through a step" is the training-systems design-review opener. The strong candidate gives the four phases with the 2N/4N split. The candidate does the optimizer-state arithmetic (8 bytes/param for AdamW) unprompted. The candidate explains why a 7B model needs sharding. "Optimizer states are the largest resident" is the sentence that shows you have sized a real run.

Key takeaways

  • One step: forward (~2N/token), loss, backward (~4N/token), AdamW update. Total ~6N FLOPs per token.
  • Step time = 6 x N x tokens-per-batch / cluster throughput. Token budget fixes the step count. Throughput is everything.
  • Memory: optimizer states (8 bytes/param) dominate weights (2) and gradients (2). 7B needs ~85 GB before activations.
  • Accumulation bridges micro-batch (fits on GPU) and batch (what the optimizer sees). Clipping bounds single-step damage.
Forward link: Volume 6 shards every resident in the memory table across GPUs. The next chapter here controls the step size itself: the learning-rate schedule.

How to read this diagram

  1. Top bar: the theoretical peak: 312 TFLOPS in FP16. No run reaches this.
  2. Bottom bar: what a good run actually sustains: 125 TFLOPS, which is 40% of peak.
  3. Formula: MFU equals achieved throughput divided by peak throughput.
  4. Rule: 40% is a good run. Below 30%, fix the data pipeline and communication before buying more GPUs.

How to read this diagram

  1. Top bar: one parameter, 12 bytes. Blue is the weight, amber the gradient, green and teal the two AdamW states.
  2. Bottom bars: the same split scaled to 7 billion parameters.
  3. The surprise: the optimizer states (56 GB) dwarf the weights (14 GB).
  4. Why it matters: this is the memory math behind Figure 4.4. It is why training needs far more memory than inference.

5. Learning-rate schedules: warmup and cosine decay

How big a step to take, and when. The schedule that keeps thousand-GPU runs alive.

Chapter 4's loop nudges every parameter once per step, but by how much? The step size is the learning rate. At LLM scale the wrong schedule kills runs. This chapter covers warmup and cosine decay, and why the schedule exists.

Design prompt

  • "Draw the standard LLM learning-rate schedule. Why the warmup? Why cosine decay?"
  • "What happens if you skip warmup on a large run?"
  • "Why decay to 10% of peak instead of zero?"

Step 1: the learning-rate schedule

The learning rate scales every optimizer update: how far each parameter moves per step. A schedule varies it over training. The near-universal LLM schedule has two phases. First warmup: the learning rate ramps linearly from 0 to its peak over the first few hundred to few thousand steps. Then cosine decay: it follows a cosine curve down to about 10% of peak by the end of training.

How to read this diagram

  1. Amber region (warmup): the learning rate climbs linearly from 0 to peak over 500 steps (illustrative count). Real runs use a small fraction of total steps. The model takes increasingly confident steps as its internal statistics stabilize.
  2. Blue curve (cosine decay): after warmup, the rate follows half a cosine wave down to 0.1 x peak. It falls slowly at first (most learning happens here), then steeply, then flattens into fine-tuning territory.
  3. Why not decay to zero: the final 10% keeps the model plastic enough to keep learning from the last tokens without thrashing. Decaying to exactly zero freezes the model early and wastes the tail of the run.

Step 2: why warmup exists

At initialization, everything is wrong at once. Weights are random. Adam's momentum and variance estimates are zero (Volume 3). The first batches produce huge, noisy gradients. A full-size step in this state can throw parameters into a region the model never recovers from. Loss spikes or diverges in the first hours.

That wastes the most expensive part of cluster setup. Warmup starts with tiny steps while the optimizer's statistics spin up and the weights find a sane region, then hands over full control. It is a few hundred steps of caution protecting months of compute.

How to read this diagram

  1. Left: full steps from step 0, gradient noise huge and chaotic, the divergence story.
  2. Right: the learning rate ramps 0 to peak (green line) while gradient magnitudes settle (teal bars).
  3. The takeaway: a few hundred steps of caution protect months of compute. Skipping warmup on a large run typically means divergence within the first percent of training.

Step 3: why cosine decay works

Two intuitions, both true. Optimization: large steps early explore and escape bad regions. Small steps late settle into the minimum without bouncing out. The cosine shape spends most of the run in the middle range, then anneals. Empirical: across thousands of runs, cosine decay to ~10% beats constant learning rates and beats linear decay on final loss. The schedule's endpoint matters too.

The decay is usually planned to hit its minimum exactly when the token budget runs out. That way no training happens at a mismatched rate. Changing the total step count mid-run without re-planning the schedule is a classic operational mistake.

What breaks without it: skip warmup on a large model. The typical outcome is divergence within the first percent of training. Loss explodes, gradients go NaN, the run is dead. Skip decay (constant LR) and the model plateaus above its achievable loss, having bounced around the minimum instead of settling. Both failure modes are expensive because teams discover them after the cluster is already burning money.
Common misunderstanding: the learning rate is a minor hyperparameter you tune at the end. At LLM scale the schedule is critical infrastructure, decided before the run and rarely changed during it. Reviewers ask about it because it separates people who have trained models from people who have read about training. The warmup-divergence story is something you learn by watching a run die, not from a textbook.
Field relevance: schedule questions are short and diagnostic. The strong candidate draws warmup + cosine from memory. The candidate gives the Adam-statistics argument for warmup. The candidate knows teams plan the schedule against the total token budget. "The decay endpoint must match the run length" is the operational detail that signals experience.

Key takeaways

  • Standard schedule: linear warmup (0 to peak over ~0.1-1% of steps), then cosine decay to ~10% of peak.
  • Warmup protects the run while Adam's statistics initialize and weights leave the random region. Skipping it risks early divergence.
  • Cosine decay: big steps explore early, small steps settle late. Plan the endpoint against the total token budget.
Forward link: the next chapter teaches you to read the loss curve this schedule produces. It shows how to tell a healthy run from a dying one at a glance.

How to read this diagram

  1. Left (red): 14 gradient samples from a small batch. They point in different directions. The mean is unreliable.
  2. Right (green): 14 samples from a large batch. They agree. The mean is trustworthy.
  3. Thick arrows: the mean of the samples: the direction the optimizer steps.
  4. Lesson: tune the learning rate and the batch size together. A big batch with a tiny learning rate wastes the clean signal.

How to read this diagram

  1. The blue curve: half a cosine wave from peak down to 0.1 x peak. The dashed amber line marks the endpoint.
  2. Left annotation: the explore phase, big steps escaping bad regions. Right annotation: the settle phase, small steps staying in the minimum.
  3. The takeaway: the schedule's endpoint must match the run length. Changing the step count mid-run without re-planning the schedule is a classic operational mistake.

6. Reading loss curves: healthy vs sick training

The loss curve is the patient's chart. Learn to read it before you touch a run.

Chapter 5's schedule shapes the loss curve step by step. This chapter teaches you to read that curve: the vital signs of a run, healthy versus sick, at a glance.

Design prompt

  • "Sketch a healthy pre-training loss curve. Now sketch three ways it can go wrong, and for each, name the cause and the fix."
  • "Loss falls smoothly but slowly, plateauing high. What are the candidate causes?"
  • "Your eval loss diverges from train loss late in training. What does that mean at LLM scale?"

Step 1: the two curves that matter

The loss curve plots training loss (Chapter 1) against step number. It is the primary vital sign of a run. It is cheap to log and available every step. It is the first place every practitioner looks when something feels wrong. Learning to read it is a core research-engineer skill. At scale you cannot inspect the model directly.

The curve is your window.

How to read this diagram

  1. Blue curve: training loss. Teal curve: eval loss, tracking just above it.
  2. The amber arrow: the generalization gap, small and steady in a healthy run.
  3. The takeaway: if eval loss rises while train loss falls, something structural is wrong. Suspect data leakage between train and eval, or the eval set drifting off-distribution.

Step 2: the four shapes

How to read this diagram

  1. Healthy (green): loss falls steeply, then gradually. The noise (jitter between steps) shrinks as training progresses. The shrinking noise means gradients stabilize: the model converges, it does not wander.

  2. Divergence (red): falls, then climbs and keeps climbing. The optimizer undoes its own work. Causes: learning rate too high for this stage, a corrupted data batch, or numerical instability. Action: stop. Roll back to the last good checkpoint. A checkpoint is a saved copy of the model weights, written every N steps precisely for this.

    Lower the LR or fix the data, then resume.

  3. Spike (amber): a sudden vertical jump, then (usually) recovery toward the trend. A bad batch, a rare numerical event, or a hardware glitch. Small spikes often self-heal. Large or repeated spikes mean rollback territory.
  4. High plateau (blue): falls fast, then flatlines well above where it should be. The model stopped learning, not finished learning. Causes: learning rate too low, decayed too fast, a bug freezing part of the network, or data too easy/repetitive.

What the axes hide: these are training loss curves. Eval loss on held-out text should track training loss closely in single-epoch pre-training (the model sees each token once, so classic overfitting is rare). If eval loss rises while train loss falls, something structural is wrong: data leakage between train and eval, or the eval set drifting off-distribution.

Step 3: diagnosis table

ShapeLikely causeWhat practitioners do
Sudden spike, recoversBad data batch, rare numerical eventWatch. If it recovers within a few hundred steps, note it and continue. Gradient clipping (Chapter 4) limits the damage.
Repeated spikesLearning rate too high, unstable data pipeline, precision issuesRoll back to pre-spike checkpoint, reduce LR, audit the data loader. The PaLM team documented this exact protocol. On the 540B run they saw about 20 loss spikes. The PaLM team handled each by restarting from roughly 100 steps before the spike and skipping 200-500 batches (Chowdhery et al., 2022).
Steady climb (divergence)LR far too high, divergence properStop the run. Roll back. This one does not self-heal.
Plateau too highLR too low or decayed too early, under-capacity, data problemCheck the schedule first (Chapter 5), then data quality (Chapter 2), then model config. The cheapest bugs live here.
Loss NaNNumerical overflow: often a bad batch through an unstable opRoll back past the NaN, skip or fix the offending batches, consider whether precision or clipping needs attention.

How to read this diagram

  1. Each row: the shape seen on the curve, the likely cause, and what practitioners do about it.
  2. Bottom strip: the calibration numbers, loss starts near 10.4 for a 32k vocabulary and lands near 1.8 to 2.2 at finish.
  3. The takeaway: still above 8 at 10% of training means something is wrong. Look at the schedule, the data, or the model config, in that order.

Step 4: what the numbers mean

Calibrate your eye: with a 32k vocabulary, loss starts near 10.4 (Chapter 1's uniform baseline). After warmup it should fall through 6-7. Mid-training, 3-4. A finished base model lands near 1.8-2.2 on held-out text. If your run's loss at 10% of training is still above 8, something is wrong. Look at the schedule, the data, or the model config, in that order.

Common misunderstanding: "smoothly falling loss means the model gets smarter." Loss measures next-token prediction on the training distribution. That correlates with capabilities but is not the same thing. A model can memorize its way to lower loss without generalizing. Benchmark performance can stall while loss still falls. That is why serious runs track eval suites alongside loss (Volume 7 covers evals properly). Loss tells you training works.

Evals tell you it is worth something.

Field relevance: loss-curve reading is the closest thing to a clinical skill in ML design reviews. The strong candidate sketches all four shapes from memory. The candidate pairs each with a cause and an action. The candidate quotes the calibration numbers (10.4 start, ~2 finish). "Small spikes often self-heal. Repeated spikes mean rollback" is the judgment call reviewers want to hear.

Key takeaways

  • Healthy: smooth fall, shrinking noise. Sick: divergence (climb), spikes (jumps), high plateau, NaN.
  • Small spikes: watch. Repeated spikes or divergence: roll back to a checkpoint, fix LR or data, resume.
  • Calibrate: ~10.4 at start (32k vocab), ~2 at finish. Still above 8 at 10% of training means something is wrong.
  • Loss measures training working, not the model being capable. Track evals alongside (Volume 7).
Forward link: the next chapter makes the loss predictable. Scaling laws turn the y-axis of these curves into arithmetic for planning billion-dollar runs.

How to read this diagram

  1. Blue: train loss. It falls for the whole run.
  2. Amber: eval loss on held-out text. It falls, bottoms out, then climbs.
  3. Red bracket: the generalization gap at one moment: how much worse the model does on unseen text.
  4. Dashed line: overfitting starts here. Train keeps improving. Eval gets worse. Stop here, or regularize.

7. Scaling laws: Kaplan, Chinchilla, and the 6ND rule

Loss is predictable. Compute is fungible. Here is the arithmetic that plans billion-dollar runs.

Chapter 6 reads one run's loss curve. This chapter predicts them all. Scaling laws turn loss into arithmetic, so billion-dollar runs get planned on spreadsheets instead of vibes.

Design prompt

  • "State the Chinchilla finding in one sentence. How many tokens per parameter is compute-optimal?"
  • "Derive the 6ND rule for training FLOPs. Compute the FLOPs for GPT-3."
  • "You have 1e24 FLOPs. What size model do you train, on how much data? Show the work."

Step 1: loss as a predictable formula

Scaling laws are empirical formulas relating test loss to three inputs. Model size N (parameters). Dataset size D (tokens). Training compute C (FLOPs, floating-point operations, the standard unit of compute). The landmark finding, across both major papers, is that loss falls as a power law in each. A power law means loss is proportional to the input raised to a negative exponent.

On a log-log plot it is a straight line. There are no sudden jumps within the studied range. If you know the curves, you can predict the loss of a 10x-larger run before spending the money. You can also split a fixed compute budget optimally between "bigger model" and "more data".

L(x) = A · x-alpha
where: L is test loss. x is one of N (parameters), D (tokens), or C (FLOPs). A and alpha are constants fit from small runs. alpha > 0. A steeper alpha means faster improvement with scale. On a log-log plot this is a straight line, because log L = log A - alpha log x.

How to read this diagram

  1. The axes: log of the input on the horizontal, log of loss on the vertical.
  2. The line: the fitted power law. Fit A and alpha on small runs, extrapolate to the big run before spending.
  3. The takeaway: no sudden jumps in the studied range, so loss is predictable, which is what makes billion-dollar runs plannable.

Step 2: why: the million-dollar planning problem

Training runs cost millions of dollars and take months. Guessing the right model size is not an option at that price. Scaling laws turn architecture choice into arithmetic. Fit the curves on small runs (millions of dollars). Extrapolate to the target run (hundreds of millions). Read off the optimal N and D.

They are the reason labs can plan frontier training runs with spreadsheets instead of vibes.

How to read this diagram

  1. Amber box: the Kaplan answer, N huge and D small. Gopher, 280B on 300B tokens, lived here.
  2. Green box: the Chinchilla answer, N and D growing equally. Chinchilla, 70B on 1.4T tokens, won at equal FLOPs.
  3. The takeaway: Chinchilla did not say small models beat big models. It said for a fixed dollar budget, a smaller model trained on much more data beats a bigger model trained on little data.

Step 3: Kaplan vs Chinchilla

Kaplan et al. (2020, OpenAI)Hoffmann et al. (2022, DeepMind): Chinchilla
SetupVaried N, D, C independently. Fit power laws for loss vs each.Trained 400+ models from 70M to 16B params, varying N and D jointly at fixed compute budgets. Fit the compute-optimal frontier directly.
Headline conclusionLoss depends mostly on N and C, weakly on D past a point. The implication drawn at the time: train the biggest model you can afford. Do not bother training it for very long.Kaplan's data-side conclusion was wrong for the jointly-optimal regime. At fixed compute, N and D should scale equally: double the model, double the data.
Rule of thumbBigger models, early stopping.~20 tokens per parameter. A 70B model wants ~1.4T tokens. A 7B model wants ~140B tokens.
Signature experimentPower-law fits across scales.Chinchilla (70B, 1.4T tokens) beat Gopher (280B, 300B tokens) on nearly every benchmark at the same training compute, despite being 4x smaller. The field calls Gopher massively undertrained: 300B/280B is about 1 token per parameter.
Key idea: Chinchilla did not say "small models beat big models". It said: for a fixed dollar budget, a smaller model trained on much more data beats a bigger model trained on little data. The 70B-vs-280B upset is the most famous controlled experiment in LLM history. "20 tokens per parameter" is the number reviewers expect you to know.
D = 20 · N
where: D is training tokens, N is the parameter count. Worked: a 70B model wants 20 x 70 x 109 = 1.4 x 1012 tokens. A 7B model wants 20 x 7 x 109 = 140 x 109 tokens. This is the "20 tokens per parameter" rule from the table above.

How to read this diagram

  1. Axes are log-log: horizontal is training FLOPs, vertical is optimal parameter count. A straight line here means a power-law relationship.
  2. Three colored lines (Approaches 1-3): the paper estimated the optimal frontier three independent ways (fixing model sizes and varying data, fitting loss curves, fitting a parametric model). They agree, which is why the field trusted the result.
  3. Dashed line (Kaplan et al. 2020): the earlier recommendation. It sits far above: at the same compute, Kaplan prescribes much bigger models on much less data.
  4. Star markers: real models. GPT-3 (175B) and Gopher (280B) sit near the Kaplan line: undertrained by Chinchilla's standard. Chinchilla (70B) sits on the new frontier: same compute as Gopher, far better loss.
  5. The blue dots: the 400+ small training runs the frontier was fit from. The extrapolation to 70B held, which is the point of scaling laws.

Step 4: the 6ND rule, derived

Training compute for a transformer is well approximated by one equation:

C = 6 · N · D
where: C is training compute in FLOPs. N is the parameter count. D is the number of training tokens. The 6 is 2 (forward) + 4 (backward) FLOPs per parameter per token, derived below.

The derivation:

  1. Forward pass: ~2N FLOPs per token. Each parameter participates in roughly one multiply and one accumulate per token it processes. (Attention adds a term quadratic in sequence length, but for standard contexts it is small next to the parameter term.)
  2. Backward pass: ~4N FLOPs per token. Backprop needs gradients with respect to both the activations and the weights, roughly twice the forward work.
  3. Total: 6N per token, times D tokens. Optimizer overhead and recomputation add corrections, but 6ND is accurate within ~10% and is the industry's standard estimate.
C = 6 x N x D

GPT-3:       6 x 175e9 x 300e9  = 3.15e23 FLOPs   (paper reports 3.14e23)
Chinchilla:  6 x 70e9  x 1.4e12 = 5.88e23 FLOPs   (same ballpark as Gopher's 5.04e23:
                                                   6 x 280e9 x 300e9, the "same compute" claim)
LLaMA-2 70B: 6 x 70e9  x 2.0e12 = 8.40e23 FLOPs   (2T tokens, slightly past Chinchilla-optimal;
                                                   later work suggests optimal may be even MORE data)
Worked example: GPT-3's FLOPs, step by step. C = 6 x 175 x 109 x 300 x 109 = 6 x 175 x 300 x 1018 = 315,000 x 1018 = 3.15 x 1023 FLOPs. The paper reports 3.14 x 1023: the one-equation estimate lands within a percent.

Note the last line: LLaMA-2 70B trained on 2T tokens (28 per parameter), and LLaMA-3 70B on 15T tokens. The field has drifted past 20 toward more data, because inference is forever. Training longer amortizes over billions of served tokens. Chinchilla optimizes training compute. If you expect heavy inference use, overtraining is rational. This nuance is a strong field signal.

Step 5: worked compute budget

You have C = 1e24 FLOPs. What do you train? Combine C = 6ND with the Chinchilla ratio D = 20N:

C = 6 x N x 20N = 120 N^2
N = sqrt(C / 120) = sqrt(1e24 / 120) = sqrt(8.33e21) ~ 9.1e10  ->  ~91B parameters
D = 20 x 91B ~ 1.8T tokens

Check: 6 x 91e9 x 1.8e12 = 9.8e23 ~ 1e24.  Consistent.

Now convert to wall-clock. An A100 does 312 TFLOPs/s in fp16 dense math. Real large runs sustain roughly 40-50% of that (MFU, model FLOPs utilization; illustrative range). On 1,024 A100s at 45% MFU: 1024 x 312e12 x 0.45 = 1.44e17 FLOP/s. Time = 1e24 / 1.44e17 = 6.9e6 seconds = 80 days. That is the shape of frontier planning: one equation for the split, one division for the calendar.

Common misunderstanding: "scaling laws prove bigger is always better." They prove loss is predictable, which is different. They predict next-token loss, not downstream capabilities, not reasoning, not truthfulness. The smooth curves describe the average over many runs. Individual capabilities can still appear abruptly (the "emergence" debate lives in Volume 11). Quote scaling laws for loss and budgets, never as a guarantee about what the model will be able to do.

Field relevance: scaling laws are the research-engineer design-review topic. The strong candidate states "20 tokens per parameter". The candidate derives 6ND on the board. The candidate computes a real model's FLOPs from memory (GPT-3: 3.15e23). The candidate works a budget split live. The overtraining-for-inference nuance separates the well-read from the rest.

Chinchilla optimizes training compute, but LLaMA-3 went past it deliberately.

Key takeaways

  • Loss follows power laws in N, D, C. Fit small, extrapolate big, plan the run with arithmetic.
  • Chinchilla: scale N and D together, ~20 tokens per parameter. The field calls Gopher (280B, 300B tokens) undertrained. Chinchilla (70B, 1.4T) won at equal compute.
  • Training FLOPs = 6ND (2N forward + 4N backward per token).
  • Wall-clock = FLOPs / (GPUs x per-GPU throughput x MFU). A 1e24-FLOP run is ~91B params on 1.8T tokens, ~80 days on 1,024 A100s.
  • Chinchilla optimizes training compute. Heavy inference use justifies overtraining past 20 tok/param.
Forward link: the next chapter strings everything so far into the narrative of a full run. It shows what actually happens, week by week, when all of this is real and the cluster costs real money.

How to read this diagram

  1. Top: the two models. Same training compute. Gopher is 4x larger.
  2. Bottom: tokens per parameter, drawn to scale.
  3. Red sliver: Gopher, about 1 token per parameter. Undertrained.
  4. Green bar: Chinchilla, 20 tokens per parameter. This is the ratio to plan around.

How to read this diagram

  1. Read left to right: combine the two equations, solve for N, solve for D, convert to wall-clock.
  2. Bottom: the consistency check, 6 x 91e9 x 1.8e12 lands back at about 1e24.
  3. The takeaway: frontier planning is one equation for the split and one division for the calendar.

8. Anatomy of a real pre-training run, week by week

What multi-week training actually looks like from the operator's chair.

Chapters 1 through 7 were the components. This chapter strings them into the narrative of a full run. It shows what actually happens, week by week, when all of it is real and the cluster costs real money.

Design prompt

  • "Narrate a pre-training run from launch to finish. What are you watching, and what do you do when the loss spikes in week 3?"
  • "Why do teams keep 24/7 on-call during large runs? What breaks at 3am?"
  • "When do you stop a run early, and when do you push through a problem?"

Honesty marker: no lab publishes a minute-by-minute diary of a frontier run. What follows is a composite reconstruction from practitioner accounts, postmortems, and documented incidents.

It includes the PaLM paper's documented incident protocol. On the 540B run they saw about 20 loss spikes. The team handled each by restarting from roughly 100 steps before the spike and skipping 200-500 batches. The shapes are real. The specific week numbers are illustrative.

Step 1: the narrative, week by week

How to read this diagram

  1. Warmup region: loss falls fast from ~10. The team watches gradient norms and loss scale, not just loss: healthy norms mean the optimizer statistics initialize correctly.
  2. First spike (~step 1500): a bad data batch. The team rolls back to the pre-spike checkpoint, skips the offending batches, and resumes training. A day lost, not a month.
  3. Steady middle: the long grind. Loss falls slowly and smoothly. The job is monitoring: dashboards, eval checkpoints every few days, data pipeline health.
  4. Second spike (~step 3800): bigger. Response escalates: gradient clipping tightened, learning rate lowered slightly, resume from checkpoint. This is the incident that pages someone.
  5. Cosine tail: loss still falling as the schedule anneals. The run ends when the token budget is spent, not when loss stops falling. The checkpoints that ship come from the tail.
WEEK 0   Setup. Data pipeline verified end to end (Ch 2-3). Small shakedown
         runs at 1% scale confirm the model, loss, and schedule behave.
         Checkpointing tested: kill a shakedown run, resume, confirm
         bitwise-identical continuation. On-call rotation starts.

WEEK 1   Launch. Warmup (Ch 5). Loss 10.4 -> ~6. The team watches gradient
         norms more than loss: exploding norms in week 1 mean the warmup
         or init is wrong, and it is cheapest to restart now.

WEEK 2   First incident. Loss spike at day 10: a corrupted data shard.
         Roll back 500 steps, blacklist the shard, resume. Total cost: a day.
         Lesson the team re-learns every run: the data pipeline (Ch 2) is
         part of the model.

WEEKS 3-5  Steady state. Loss 4 -> 2.5, noise shrinking. Eval checkpoints
         twice a week: perplexity on held-out sets, a few benchmark probes.
         Hardware failures happen (a GPU dies every few days at this scale);
         checkpointing (Volume 6) makes each one a 30-minute resume, not a
         disaster. The on-call rotation exists for these.

WEEK 6   Second incident. Repeated spikes, bigger this time. Diagnosis:
         learning rate slightly too hot for this phase plus a precision
         edge case. Fix: roll back, lower peak LR 15%, tighten clipping,
         resume. The run loses two days. The alternative (pushing through)
         risked full divergence and losing weeks.

WEEKS 7-8  Cosine tail. Loss 2.2 -> 1.9, still falling. Final evals.
         The run stops when the token budget (Ch 7) is exhausted.
         Checkpoints are frozen, evaluated, and handed to post-training.
         The cluster is released. The team sleeps.

Step 2: failure modes and the operator's playbook

FailureSignalResponse
Loss spikeVertical jump on the curve (Ch 6)Small: watch. Large/repeated: roll back to checkpoint, skip bad data or lower LR, resume.
DivergenceLoss climbing steadilyStop. Roll back. Fix LR/schedule/data. Never push through.
Hardware failureDead GPU/node, NCCL timeout (NCCL is the GPU communication library; Volume 6)Resume from checkpoint on spare nodes. That is why checkpointing (Volume 6) is non-negotiable.
Data pipeline stallSteps slow down, GPUs starveFix the loader/pipeline. Starved GPUs burn money doing nothing. Data throughput is a first-class metric.
Gradient norm explosionNorm chart spikes before loss doesEarly warning of instability. Tighten clipping, check LR, consider rollback.

The through-line: training at scale is operations. The team decides the research (architecture, data, schedule) before launch. The run itself is monitoring, incident response, and judgment calls about when to intervene. Teams staff it like operations because it is operations: dashboards, alerts, runbooks, on-call. The romantic image of "set hyperparameters and wait" dies the first time a $10M run spikes at 3am.

Common misunderstanding: "once training starts, it is automatic." The first 5% and any incident are hands-on. The team decides checkpoint discipline, rollback criteria, and escalation rules before launch. Deciding them during a 3am spike is how runs die. Questions about "your experience with large runs" are really asking whether you understand this operational reality.
Field relevance: run-narrative questions test operational maturity. The strong candidate tells the week-by-week story fluently. The candidate names the rollback decision explicitly. The cost of a day beats the risk of divergence. The candidate explains 24/7 on-call as a response to hardware failure rates and spike response times. Mentioning the PaLM paper's documented restart protocol shows you read primary sources.

Key takeaways

  • A run is: shakedown, warmup, steady state with incidents, cosine tail. The token budget decides the end.
  • Spikes: roll back, fix, resume. Divergence: stop. Hardware: resume from checkpoint. Data stall: fix the pipeline.
  • Large-scale training is operations: dashboards, on-call, runbooks, decided-before-launch rollback criteria.
  • Checkpointing is what makes every failure recoverable. (Full treatment: Volume 6.)
Forward link: the run produces a base model. The next chapter is the honest accounting of what that model is and is not. Volume 6 explains the distributed machinery that made the run possible.

How to read this diagram

  1. Each row: the failure, the signal on the dashboards, and the response.
  2. Bottom: the through-line. Teams decide these before launch, not during the 3am spike.
  3. The takeaway: training at scale is operations. Checkpoint discipline, rollback criteria, and escalation rules are what keep a multi-million-dollar run alive.

9. The honest boundary: what pre-training is and is not

A base model predicts text. It does not follow instructions, and it is not aligned. Know the line.

Chapter 8's run produced a trained base model. This chapter is the honest accounting of what that product is, and what it is not.

Design prompt

  • "What is a base model? What can it do, and what will it fail at?"
  • "Show me with an example why a base model does not 'answer questions'."
  • "What changes in post-training? Name the stages and what each one fixes."

Step 1: what pre-training is and is not

A base model is the direct product of pre-training: a machine that assigns probabilities to continuations of text. It has absorbed grammar, facts, code patterns, and reasoning traces from its trillions of tokens. But it has one behavior: continue the text. It has no concept of instructions, no notion of being helpful, and no preference for truth over plausible-sounding text. Everything useful it does emerges from pattern continuation. Everything it fails at fails for the same reason.

How to read this diagram

  1. Left column (this volume): the base model. Given a prompt, it continues in the style of its training data. Few-shot prompting works because the pattern "examples, then task" appears in training data. It does not understand the task. It continues the pattern.
  2. Right column (Volume 7): post-training. Instruction tuning teaches the model to treat prompts as instructions. RLHF/RLAIF shapes its preferences. Safety training teaches refusals. The assistant behavior users know lives here, not in pre-training.
  3. The gap between columns: training teaches everything the right column does that the left cannot. None of it emerges. A base model will not refuse harmful requests. It will not ask clarifying questions. It will happily continue a prompt into nonsense if the pattern suggests it.

Step 2: what a base model does well, and where it breaks

BehaviorBase modelWhy
Complete a sentenceExcellentThat is literally the training objective.
Few-shot pattern tasksGood, with examples in the promptThe pattern "examples then task" is in the data. Continuation does the rest.
Answer a direct questionUnreliableIt continues the question the way training text continues questions: often with another question, a quiz, or trivia. It was never trained to answer.
Follow multi-step instructionsPoorInstructions are a behavior, not a text pattern. Continuation has no notion of obedience.
Refuse harmful requestsWill notRefusal is a trained preference, not a property of text continuation.
Admit uncertaintyWill notTraining rewards plausible continuation, which includes confident-sounding text. Calibration is not in the objective.

The demo that makes this visceral: prompt a base model with "Q: What is the capital of France? A:". It often answers correctly ("Paris"), because Q/A patterns are in the data. Then prompt "Q: What is the capital of France?" alone. It may continue with "Q: What is the capital of Spain?". It continues a quiz. It does not answer you.

Same model, same knowledge, different behavior, because behavior is pattern-matching all the way down.

How to read this diagram

  1. Left: with 'A:' the model continues the Q/A pattern correctly.
  2. Right: without it, the same knowledge continues as a quiz. Same model, same knowledge, different behavior.
  3. The takeaway: a base model does not answer questions. It continues text. Instruction-following is a post-training behavior, the subject of Volume 7.

Step 3: what post-training adds

Post-training, the subject of Volume 7, builds the assistant on top of the base model:

  • Instruction tuning: supervised training on (instruction, response) pairs. Teaches the model the format of assistance: prompts are instructions, responses should address them.
  • Preference training (RLHF / RLAIF): training on human (or AI) judgments of which response is better. Shapes preferences: helpfulness, honesty, style. This is where "the model tries to be helpful" comes from.
  • Safety training: refusals, harm avoidance, policy behavior. Entirely post-training. A base model has none of it.
  • Reasoning training: chain-of-thought and related methods that teach the model to work through problems step by step. The modern reasoning models are largely a post-training achievement built on pre-trained bases.

The honest framing: pre-training builds capabilities (knowledge, patterns, representations). Post-training builds behavior (instruction-following, helpfulness, safety). Most of what users experience as "the model" is post-training behavior riding on pre-trained capability. Confusing the two is the most common conceptual error in discussions of LLM abilities.

Common misunderstanding: pre-training makes the model smart, post-training just makes it polite. Post-training changes behavior profoundly: reasoning, tool use, instruction-following, and refusal are all substantially post-training achievements. And pre-training is not "just" anything: the base model's knowledge and representations are the ceiling everything else builds on. Post-training cannot turn a weak base into a strong model. Both stages are critical. They build different things.
Field relevance: the boundary question is a conceptual filter. The strong candidate gives the Q/A demo ("continuing a quiz, not answering you"). The candidate distinguishes capabilities from behavior cleanly. The candidate names the post-training stages unprompted. "Most of what users experience is post-training behavior on pre-trained capability" is the one-liner.

Key takeaways

  • A base model continues text. It does not follow instructions, refuse, or admit uncertainty: those are post-training behaviors.
  • Few-shot prompting works by pattern continuation, not understanding. Change the pattern and the behavior changes.
  • Post-training (Volume 7): instruction tuning (format), preference training (helpfulness), safety (refusals), reasoning training.
  • Pre-training builds capabilities. Post-training builds behavior. Both are critical.
Forward link: Volume 7 is post-training: instruction tuning, RLHF, and how the assistant is actually built. Volume 6 is the distributed machinery that makes runs like Chapter 8's possible.

How to read this diagram

  1. Left: one benchmark question.
  2. Middle: the question is cut into overlapping 13-word chunks.
  3. Right: the pipeline searches each chunk in the training crawl.
  4. Red: a chunk matches, so the pipeline removes the text.
  5. Green: no chunk matches, so the text stays. Paraphrases still slip through.

Capstone: train a tiny GPT and watch the loss fall

Executed lab: a tiny GPT trained on this machine (PyTorch 2.14.0 CPU), 818,176 parameters, 2000 steps on Tiny Shakespeare.

Executed on this machine: the run below is real output from a Karpathy-style character-level tiny GPT on Tiny Shakespeare (1,115,394 chars). It trained on this machine's CPU in September 2026. Your numbers will differ slightly (random init, no seed fixed). The shape of the curve will not.

Part A: the model (from Volumes 1-4)

# Tiny GPT: 4 layers, 4 heads, 128 dims, character-level vocab (65 chars).
# Assemble from earlier volumes: embeddings (V4 Ch2), causal attention
# (V4 Ch3-4), MLP with GELU (V4 Ch7), pre-norm blocks (V4 Ch7), trained with
# next-token cross-entropy (this volume, Ch1), AdamW.
# Corpus: Tiny Shakespeare (1,115,394 chars), the standard toy for this recipe.

# Training config (executed on this machine, PyTorch 2.14.0 CPU):
batch_size = 32        # sequences per micro-batch
block_size = 64        # context length (tokens per sequence)
max_iters = 2000
lr_warmup = 100        # warmup steps (Ch 5)
lr_peak = 3e-4
lr_final = 3e-5        # cosine decay to 10% (Ch 5)

# Real loss trajectory (character-level, vocab 65; uniform = ln(65) = 4.17):
#   step 0:     4.325  (random init, near the uniform baseline)
#   step 99:    2.862  (warmup done; basic character statistics learned)
#   step 499:   2.330  (common words emerging)
#   step 999:   2.004  (phrases and Shakespearean names appearing)
#   step 1999:  1.899  (final valid loss 2.008; readable babble)

# Real 120-char sample after 2000 steps:
#   DUKENRO
#   TENTUS:
#   My the leaddne ast imponiess, be upory
#   Andy to to goowh, Ik noten: of warch,
#   Cife my ampey hillood by a

Part B: experiments (this volume's concepts, made tangible)

  1. Vary the learning rate. Run at 3e-4, 3e-3, and 3e-5. The 3e-3 run should show Chapter 6's divergence or violent spikes. 3e-5 should plateau high and slow. Plot all three loss curves on one axis. This is the cheapest possible demonstration of why the schedule matters.
  2. Kill the warmup. Start at peak LR from step 0 with everything else identical. Watch the first 50 steps: gradient norms spike, loss jumps. Re-enable warmup and compare. Chapter 5's story in one plot.
  3. Shrink the batch. Halve the batch size (keeping total tokens fixed by doubling steps). The loss curve gets noisier but reaches a similar endpoint: the gradient-accumulation argument from Chapter 3, verified empirically.
  4. Measure the 6ND rule. Count your model's parameters. Multiply by 6 and by tokens seen. Compare the resulting FLOP estimate against your wall-clock time and your GPU's rated throughput. You will land within ~2x, which makes Chapter 7's planning arithmetic feel real.

How to read this diagram

  1. Each row: the experiment, the chapter it tests, what to vary, and the curve shape to expect.
  2. Bottom: the write-up recipe, hypothesis, plot, and what the curve taught you.
  3. The takeaway: the learning-rate experiments are the highest-value hour. Divergence and plateaus teach more than any chapter.

Part C: what to write up

One page. Your loss curve, with the four Chapter 6 shapes labeled where they appear. The calibration check (did step 0 land near ln(vocab size)?). One paragraph on which experiment surprised you and why. If nothing surprised you, you did not push the learning rate hard enough.

Capstone takeaways

  • A tiny GPT reproduces every phenomenon in this volume: warmup, spikes, plateaus, the uniform-loss baseline.
  • The learning-rate experiments are the highest-value hour: divergence and plateaus teach more than any chapter.
  • 6ND predicts your run's cost within ~2x even at toy scale. The planning arithmetic is real.
